questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: What the ash left after burning dried leaf tissue contains, and what is lost on drying and burning
questions.question: A weighed sample of fresh leaf tissue is dried in an oven to constant mass and then burnt completely in a furnace, leaving a small amount of grey ash. Which statement about this experiment is correct?
options: A) The ash contains inorganic elements such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and phosphorus (as oxides, phosphates and similar salts); the carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen of the organic compounds escape as gases on burning
B) The ash contains the proteins and nucleic acids of the tissue, because these are large macromolecules
C) Most of the mass lost in the oven is carbon dioxide released from the organic compounds
D) The ash contains the same elements in the same proportions as the Earth's crust
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The ash contains inorganic elements such as calcium, magnesium, potassium and phosphorus; the carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen of the organic compounds escape as gases on burning.
Concept: Chemical analysis of living tissue: drying removes water (the largest single component of living tissue); burning oxidises all organic compounds to gases such as CO₂, water vapour and oxides of nitrogen. What remains (the ash) is the inorganic (mineral) part of the tissue.
Why: Calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, phosphorus and sulphur are not converted to gases at furnace temperatures; they stay as oxides, phosphates, sulphates and carbonates. All organic molecules (sugars, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids) are destroyed.
Why not the others: (B) Proteins and nucleic acids are organic and burn away; only their mineral elements (such as P and S) remain. (C) Oven drying at moderate temperature removes water, not CO₂; organic compounds are oxidised only in the furnace. (D) Living matter differs greatly from the crust; for example, carbon and hydrogen are far more abundant in living tissue.
Key point: Fresh tissue → (dry) loses water → (burn) loses C, H, N as gases → ash = inorganic minerals.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Counting peptide bonds in haemoglobin from chain data and naming its highest level of structure
questions.question:
The table gives data on the polypeptide chains of one molecule of adult human haemoglobin. Each chain folds into its own compact globular unit carrying one haem group, and the four chains are held together by non-covalent interactions.

Chain | Number in one molecule | Amino-acid residues per chain
α | 2 | 141
β | 2 | 146

How many peptide bonds are there in one haemoglobin molecule, and what is the highest level of protein structure it shows?
options: A) 574; quaternary
B) 570; tertiary
C) 287; quaternary
D) 570; quaternary
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 570; quaternary.
Concept: In a single linear polypeptide of n amino-acid residues there are n − 1 peptide bonds. Proteins have primary (sequence), secondary (helix or sheet), tertiary (3-D folding of one chain) and quaternary (arrangement of two or more chains) structure.
Why: α chains: 2 × (141 − 1) = 280 bonds; β chains: 2 × (146 − 1) = 290 bonds; total = 570. The four chains are separate polypeptides held together, so haemoglobin has quaternary structure.
Why not the others: (A) 574 is the total number of residues; each chain has one fewer peptide bond than residues. (B) The bond count is right, but a protein made of several chains shows quaternary, not just tertiary, structure. (C) 287 counts only one α and one β chain (141 + 146) and does not subtract the chain ends.
Key point: Peptide bonds = residues − number of chains; more than one chain → quaternary structure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Gametes formed when sister chromatids fail to separate in one cell at meiosis II
questions.question: In a diploid animal, meiosis I in a primary spermatocyte is normal. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate in one of the two secondary spermatocytes, while the other secondary spermatocyte divides normally. What fraction of the four sperm formed from this primary spermatocyte are abnormal, and what are their chromosome numbers (n = normal haploid number)?
options: A) All four; two with n + 1 and two with n − 1
B) Half; both with n + 1
C) Half; one with n + 1 and one with n − 1
D) One quarter; with n + 1
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Half; one with n + 1 and one with n − 1.
Concept: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis. Failure of separation (non-disjunction) gives gametes with an extra or a missing chromosome. Meiosis is significant because it halves the chromosome number exactly, keeping it constant from generation to generation; errors upset this.
Why: After a normal meiosis I, each secondary spermatocyte has n chromosomes. The normal one gives two n sperm. In the faulty one, both chromatids of one chromosome go to the same pole, giving one sperm with n + 1 and one with n − 1. So two of the four sperm are abnormal.
Why not the others: (A) All four abnormal (two n + 1, two n − 1) is the result of non-disjunction in meiosis I. (B) The chromatid missing from one cell is present in the other, so the abnormal sperm cannot both be n + 1. (D) Non-disjunction always produces a pair: one cell with the extra chromosome and one lacking it.
Key point: Non-disjunction in meiosis I → 4 of 4 abnormal; in one cell at meiosis II → 2 of 4 abnormal (n + 1 and n − 1).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why extra CO₂ raises photosynthesis in a C3 plant but hardly in a C4 plant
questions.question: In bright light at the optimum temperature, raising the CO₂ concentration of the air from about 360 to 450 µL L⁻¹ markedly increases the rate of photosynthesis of tomato (a C3 plant) but has little effect on maize (a C4 plant). What is the reason?
options: A) The stomata of maize close completely when CO₂ rises, so no extra CO₂ can enter

B) In maize, PEP carboxylase captures CO₂ and concentrates it in the bundle-sheath cells, so RuBisCO there is already nearly saturated at about 360 µL L⁻¹; in tomato, RuBisCO is not saturated and also reacts with O₂, so extra CO₂ increases carboxylation
C) At 450 µL L⁻¹ light becomes the limiting factor for tomato, but not for maize
D) Maize has no RuBisCO, so its rate does not depend on CO₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) In maize, PEP carboxylase concentrates CO₂ in the bundle-sheath cells, so RuBisCO there is already nearly saturated; in tomato, RuBisCO is unsaturated and also reacts with O₂.
Concept: Blackman's law of limiting factors: the rate is controlled by the factor in shortest supply. CO₂ is a major limiting factor in bright light. C4 plants saturate at about 360 µL L⁻¹, while C3 plants keep responding up to about 450 µL L⁻¹ or more.
Why: PEP carboxylase has a high affinity for CO₂ (as HCO₃⁻) and has no oxygenase activity. The C4 acids release CO₂ around RuBisCO in the bundle sheath, so RuBisCO works close to its maximum and photorespiration is negligible. In a C3 leaf, RuBisCO in the mesophyll is exposed to air-level CO₂, is not saturated, and loses some carbon by photorespiration; raising CO₂ favours carboxylation. This is why CO₂ enrichment is used in greenhouses for tomatoes.
Why not the others: (A) Stomata may narrow somewhat in high CO₂, but they do not close completely, and this is not why the C4 rate is unchanged. (C) If light became limiting for tomato, extra CO₂ would not raise its rate, but the observed rate does rise. (D) C4 plants have RuBisCO in their bundle-sheath cells; the Calvin cycle runs there.
Key point: C4 plants concentrate CO₂ around RuBisCO, so they saturate at lower CO₂; C3 plants respond to CO₂ enrichment.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: ATP yield of alcoholic fermentation compared with the balance sheet, and the fate of glycolytic NADH
questions.question: A yeast culture is moved from aerobic conditions to anaerobic conditions and begins alcoholic fermentation. Using the respiratory balance sheet value of 38 ATP per glucose for aerobic respiration, how many glucose molecules must be fermented to give the same net ATP as the aerobic respiration of one glucose, and what happens to the NADH formed in glycolysis during fermentation?
options: A) 19; it is oxidised by the electron transport chain
B) 19; it reduces pyruvic acid to lactic acid
C) 9.5; it reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol
D) 19; it reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, regenerating NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 19; it reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, regenerating NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue.
Concept: In fermentation, glycolysis is the only ATP-forming stage. Pyruvic acid is decarboxylated to acetaldehyde, which is reduced to ethanol by NADH. This re-forms NAD⁺, which glycolysis needs at the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate step.
Given: aerobic yield 38 ATP per glucose (balance sheet); glycolysis forms 4 ATP and uses 2 ATP per glucose.
Formula/Principle: number of glucose = aerobic ATP per glucose ÷ net fermentation ATP per glucose.
Step 1: Net ATP from fermentation = 4 − 2 = 2 per glucose.
Step 2: 38 ÷ 2 = 19 glucose molecules.
Why: Without O₂ as the final electron acceptor, the electron transport chain stops; NADH must be reoxidised in the cytoplasm, otherwise glycolysis would stop for lack of NAD⁺. No ATP is made in the conversion of pyruvate to ethanol.
Why not the others: (A) The electron transport chain needs O₂ and does not work under anaerobic conditions. (B) Lactic acid is formed in muscle and some bacteria; yeast forms ethanol and CO₂. (C) 9.5 uses the gross 4 ATP instead of the net 2 ATP from glycolysis.
Key point: Fermentation: net 2 ATP per glucose; NADH → NAD⁺ by reducing acetaldehyde to ethanol.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Order of brain regions passed by a pain signal travelling from the foot to the cerebral cortex
questions.question: A pain signal from the foot enters the spinal cord and travels up to the region of the brain where pain is consciously felt. In which order does the ascending pathway pass through the parts of the central neural system?
options: A) Spinal cord → medulla oblongata → pons → midbrain → thalamus → cerebral cortex (sensory area)
B) Spinal cord → cerebellum → pons → hypothalamus → cerebral cortex
C) Spinal cord → pons → medulla oblongata → midbrain → thalamus → cerebral cortex
D) Spinal cord → medulla oblongata → midbrain → pons → hypothalamus → cerebral cortex
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Spinal cord → medulla oblongata → pons → midbrain → thalamus → cerebral cortex (sensory area).
Concept: The brain is divided into hindbrain (medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum), midbrain, and forebrain (thalamus, hypothalamus, cerebrum). The medulla is continuous with the spinal cord. The thalamus is the main relay centre for sensory signals going to the cerebral cortex.
Why: Going upward from the spinal cord, a signal first enters the medulla, then the pons, then the midbrain, and then reaches the forebrain. There, the thalamus relays it to the sensory area of the cerebral cortex, where the sensation is perceived.
Why not the others: (B) The cerebellum controls balance and coordination and is not on this relay route; the hypothalamus regulates body temperature, hunger and hormones, and is not the sensory relay. (C) The pons lies above the medulla, so the medulla must come first. (D) The pons lies below the midbrain, and the relay to the cortex is the thalamus, not the hypothalamus.
Key point: Upward order: medulla → pons → midbrain → thalamus → cerebral cortex.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Recombination between the haemophilia and colour-blindness genes from the sons of a doubly heterozygous woman
questions.question:
A woman with normal vision and normal blood clotting had a father who suffered from both haemophilia and red–green colour blindness. She marries a man with normal vision and normal clotting. Data pooled from many such families give the phenotypes of 100 sons:

Phenotype of son | Number
Haemophilic and colour-blind | 45
Normal for both | 47
Haemophilic only | 4
Colour-blind only | 4

What is the recombination frequency between the two genes, how are the mutant alleles arranged in the mother, and what is expected among the daughters?
options: A) 8 %; the two mutant alleles are on different X chromosomes; half the daughters are colour-blind
B) 92 %; the two mutant alleles are on the same X chromosome; all daughters are normal
C) 8 %; the two mutant alleles are on the same X chromosome; all daughters have normal vision and normal clotting
D) 4 %; the two mutant alleles are on the same X chromosome; one quarter of the daughters are haemophilic
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8 %; the two mutant alleles are on the same X chromosome; all daughters have normal vision and normal clotting.
Concept: Haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked recessive. A son receives his only X from his mother, so the sons' phenotypes show directly which X chromosomes the mother made. The two parental (most frequent) classes show how the alleles were arranged; the rare classes are recombinants from crossing over.
Why: The woman got one X from her father carrying both mutant alleles, so both are on the same X. The parental classes are 45 + 47 = 92; recombinants are 4 + 4 = 8 out of 100, giving 8 %. Every daughter receives her father's normal X, which carries both dominant normal alleles, so all daughters are phenotypically normal (half are carriers of something).
Why not the others: (A) Recombinants are the rare classes, which shows the alleles are together on one X, not on different X chromosomes; daughters cannot be colour-blind with a normal father. (B) 92 % is the parental (non-recombinant) frequency. (D) Recombination frequency = all recombinants (4 + 4) ÷ total = 8 %, not 4 %; daughters cannot be haemophilic when the father is normal.
Key point: Sons reveal the mother's X chromosomes; recombination frequency = recombinant sons ÷ all sons.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia: qualitative versus quantitative globin defect
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares sickle-cell anaemia and thalassemia?
options: A) Both are X-linked recessive disorders that affect only males

B) Sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative defect, in which an abnormal β-globin is made with valine in place of glutamic acid at the sixth position (from a single base change GAG → GUG); thalassemia is a quantitative defect, in which too little of a normal globin chain is made; both are autosomal recessive
C) Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by deletion of the whole β-globin gene, while thalassemia is caused by a single base substitution
D) Sickle-cell anaemia is a quantitative defect and thalassemia is a qualitative defect
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative defect (Glu → Val at position 6 of β-globin, from GAG → GUG); thalassemia is a quantitative defect (reduced synthesis of a normal globin chain); both are autosomal recessive.
Concept: Both are inherited haemoglobin disorders on autosomes. Sickle-cell anaemia: a point mutation changes one amino acid, so the haemoglobin polymerises at low oxygen and the red cells become sickle-shaped. Thalassemia: mutation or deletion of a globin gene lowers the amount of α or β chains made, causing anaemia.
Why: The sickle-cell protein is made in normal amount but has the wrong structure (qualitative). In thalassemia, the protein made is normal but too little of it is produced (quantitative).
Why not the others: (A) Both genes are on autosomes (chromosome 11 for β-globin; chromosome 16 for α-globin), so both sexes are affected equally. (C) The causes are reversed: sickle-cell is a single substitution; thalassemia often involves deletions or mutations that reduce synthesis. (D) This swaps the qualitative and quantitative descriptions.
Key point: Sickle-cell = wrong globin (qualitative); thalassemia = too little globin (quantitative); both autosomal recessive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Comparing the sizes, gene numbers and features of the human and rice genomes
questions.question: Which statement correctly compares the human genome with the rice genome, as revealed by their genome projects?
options: A) The rice genome (about 0.4 billion bp in 12 chromosome pairs) is roughly one-eighth the size of the human genome (about 3.2 billion bp), yet it is predicted to contain more protein-coding genes than the human genome
B) In both genomes, more than half of the DNA codes for proteins
C) In humans, the Y chromosome carries the largest number of genes
D) Rice and humans have the same number of chromosomes, 2n = 46
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The rice genome (about 0.4 billion bp, 12 chromosome pairs) is about one-eighth the size of the human genome (about 3.2 billion bp), yet it is predicted to have more protein-coding genes.
Concept: The Human Genome Project found that the human genome has about 3164.7 million bp, that less than 2 % of it codes for proteins, that repeated sequences make up a large part, that chromosome 1 has the most genes (2968) and the Y chromosome the fewest (231). The rice genome (Oryza sativa, 2n = 24) was sequenced as a model cereal genome.
Why: 3.2 ÷ 0.4 ≈ 8. The rice genome is predicted to contain about 37,000–40,000 protein-coding genes, compared with roughly 20,000–30,000 in humans. So genome size and gene number do not rise together; much of the extra human DNA is non-coding and repetitive.
Why not the others: (B) Less than 2 % of the human genome codes for proteins. (C) Chromosome 1 has the most genes; the Y chromosome has the fewest. (D) Rice has 2n = 24; humans have 2n = 46.
Key point: Bigger genome ≠ more genes; most human DNA is non-coding.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Identifying the biological father from VNTR band positions in a DNA fingerprint
questions.question:
In a disputed-paternity case, DNA from a mother, her child and three men (X, Y and Z) is cut, separated by electrophoresis and probed for a VNTR. The band positions found (numbered from the top of the gel) are:

Person | Band positions
Mother | 2, 5, 7, 9
Child | 2, 4, 7, 8
Man X | 1, 4, 6, 8
Man Y | 3, 4, 5, 9
Man Z | 3, 6, 8, 10

Which man can be the biological father?
options: A) Man Y
B) Man Z
C) None of them can be identified from these data
D) Man X
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Man X.
Concept: In DNA fingerprinting, VNTRs (variable number tandem repeats) vary in length between people. A child inherits one set of chromosomes from each parent, so every band in the child must be present in the mother or the father.
Why: The child's bands 2 and 7 match the mother. The other bands, 4 and 8, must come from the father. Only man X has both band 4 and band 8.
Why not the others: (A) Man Y has band 4 but not band 8. (B) Man Z has band 8 but not band 4. (C) The data are enough: exactly one man has both of the child's non-maternal bands.
Key point: Remove the maternal bands; the father must have all of the remaining bands of the child.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Results of Pasteur's swan-neck flask experiment under three conditions
questions.question: Meat broth is boiled in three swan-neck flasks and allowed to cool. Flask P is left with its curved neck intact. In flask Q the curved neck is broken off after cooling. Flask R keeps its intact neck, but after cooling it is tilted so that the broth runs into the bend of the neck (where dust has settled) and back into the flask. Which result is expected, and what does it show?
options: A) Microbes grow in P, Q and R, which shows that life arises from non-living broth
B) Microbes grow in Q and R only, which shows that they come from pre-existing microbes carried on dust, because air could also reach the broth in P
C) Microbes grow in Q only, because the curved neck kills microbes by heating them
D) Microbes grow in none of the flasks, because boiling destroys the vital force needed for life
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Microbes grow in Q and R only, which shows that they come from pre-existing microbes carried on dust.
Concept: Louis Pasteur's experiment disproved spontaneous generation (the idea that life arises from non-living matter) and supported the idea that life comes only from pre-existing life.
Why: The open, curved neck lets air reach the broth but traps dust and microbes in its bend. P stays sterile even though air reaches it, so air itself does not create life. In Q, dust falls straight in; in R, the broth touches the trapped dust. In both, microbes grow.
Why not the others: (A) Sterile broth in P shows that broth plus air does not produce life by itself. (C) The neck does not heat anything after cooling; R, with an intact neck, also shows growth once the broth touches the trapped dust. (D) Microbes do grow in Q and R, so the broth can still support life.
Key point: Swan-neck flask: air enters but dust is trapped; broth stays sterile until it meets the dust → life from pre-existing life.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting antibody and viral-RNA tests during the window period of HIV infection
questions.question: A person had a high-risk exposure to HIV two weeks ago. An antibody-based ELISA is negative, but a test for HIV RNA in the plasma is strongly positive. Three months later both tests are positive, and the number of helper T cells has begun to fall. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) The person was not infected at two weeks; infection must have happened later
B) The RNA test at two weeks was a false positive, because ELISA is the standard test
C) At two weeks the virus was multiplying, but antibodies had not yet formed in detectable amounts (the window period); later, as HIV keeps replicating in helper T cells, their number falls
D) HIV directly destroys B lymphocytes, so antibodies never form in an infected person
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) At two weeks the virus was multiplying but antibodies were not yet detectable (window period); later, continued replication in helper T cells lowers their number.
Concept: HIV is a retrovirus. It enters macrophages and helper T lymphocytes (T_H cells), makes viral DNA by reverse transcriptase, and the infected cells release new virus. ELISA detects antibodies made against the virus, which take some weeks to appear. A test for viral RNA detects the virus itself.
Why: Early in infection, plenty of virus is present, but the B cells have not yet produced detectable antibodies. Once they do, ELISA becomes positive. As the virus continues to replicate, helper T cells are destroyed and their count falls, leading in time to immunodeficiency (AIDS).
Why not the others: (A) A strongly positive viral RNA test at two weeks shows the virus was already present. (B) The later positive ELISA confirms infection; the RNA test simply detected it earlier. (D) HIV mainly attacks helper T cells, not B cells; antibodies do form, as the positive ELISA at three months shows.
Key point: Viral RNA is detectable before antibodies appear; ELISA can be negative in the window period.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of leaving out the chromogenic substrate when screening recombinants by lacZ insertional inactivation
questions.question: A student inserts a gene into the lacZ (β-galactosidase) region of a plasmid that also carries an ampicillin-resistance gene, transforms E. coli with the ligation mixture, and spreads the cells on agar containing ampicillin. By mistake, the chromogenic substrate (X-gal) is left out of the medium. What is observed?
options: A) Only transformed cells grow, but all colonies are colourless, so recombinant colonies cannot be told apart from non-recombinant ones
B) Recombinant colonies are blue and non-recombinant colonies are colourless
C) No colonies grow, because β-galactosidase activity is needed for growth on this medium
D) Untransformed cells also grow, as colourless colonies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Only transformed cells grow, but all colonies are colourless, so recombinants cannot be distinguished.
Concept: In insertional inactivation, inserting DNA into the lacZ gene inactivates β-galactosidase. With a chromogenic substrate in the medium, colonies with an active enzyme (non-recombinants) turn blue; colonies with the insert (recombinants) stay colourless.
Why: Ampicillin still kills untransformed cells, so only plasmid-carrying cells grow. But without the substrate, no blue colour can form, so both kinds of colony look the same.
Why not the others: (B) Blue colour needs the substrate; also, it is the non-recombinants (intact lacZ) that turn blue, not the recombinants. (C) The cells do not need β-galactosidase to grow on ordinary nutrient agar with ampicillin; they need the ampicillin-resistance gene. (D) Untransformed cells lack the ampicillin-resistance gene and are killed.
Key point: Blue/colourless screening needs the chromogenic substrate; antibiotic selects transformants, colour identifies recombinants.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Interpreting age distributions of three populations as expanding, stable or declining
questions.question:
The table shows the percentage of individuals in each age group in three populations.

Population | Pre-reproductive | Reproductive | Post-reproductive
P | 45 | 40 | 15
Q | 35 | 40 | 25
R | 15 | 45 | 40

Which interpretation is correct?
options: A) P is declining, Q is stable and R is expanding
B) P is stable, Q is expanding and R is declining
C) P is expanding, Q is stable and R is declining
D) All three populations are stable, because the reproductive group is about the same size in each
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) P is expanding, Q is stable and R is declining.
Concept: An age pyramid plots the numbers in the pre-reproductive, reproductive and post-reproductive groups. A broad base (many young) means a growing (expanding) population; a base about equal to the reproductive group gives a bell-shaped (stable) pyramid; a narrow base gives an urn-shaped (declining) pyramid.
Why: P has the largest pre-reproductive group, so many individuals will soon enter the reproductive group: expanding. In Q, the young group is about the same as the reproductive group: roughly stable. In R, very few young will replace the large older groups: declining.
Why not the others: (A) This reverses P and R. (B) Q's base is not larger than its reproductive group, so it is not expanding, and P's broad base means growth, not stability. (D) The future size depends on how many young individuals there are to replace the reproductive group, which differs greatly between the populations.
Key point: Broad base → expanding; base ≈ middle → stable; narrow base → declining.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Ecological efficiency of energy transfer between trophic levels from productivity data
questions.question: In a grassland, the gross primary productivity is 25,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and plant respiration uses 5,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. The energy stored in herbivores is 2,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ and in carnivores 150 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹. What are the transfer efficiencies from producers (net primary productivity) to herbivores and from herbivores to carnivores, and what fraction of the net primary productivity reaches the carnivores?
options: B) 10 % and 7.5 %; less than 1 %
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 10 % and 7.5 %; less than 1 %.
Concept: Net primary productivity (NPP) = gross primary productivity (GPP) − respiration loss; it is the energy available to herbivores. At each step only a small part of the energy (about 10 % on average) is passed on, the rest being lost mainly as heat in respiration.
Given: GPP = 25,000; respiration = 5,000; herbivores = 2,000; carnivores = 150 (all kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹).
Formula/Principle: efficiency = energy at the higher level ÷ energy at the level below × 100 %.
Step 1: NPP = 25,000 − 5,000 = 20,000 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; herbivores: 2,000 ÷ 20,000 = 10 %.
Step 2: Carnivores: 150 ÷ 2,000 = 7.5 %; fraction of NPP reaching carnivores = 150 ÷ 20,000 = 0.75 %.
Why: The energy reaching each level falls steeply, so the pyramid of energy is always upright and food chains are short.
Why not the others: (A) Uses GPP instead of NPP as the energy available to herbivores. (C) Divides herbivore energy by carnivore energy (2,000 ÷ 150) and inverts the ratio. (D) 80 % is NPP as a fraction of GPP, not a transfer between trophic levels.
Key point: NPP = GPP − R; about 10 % transfer per step; energy pyramid is always upright.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Zones of a biosphere reserve from the centre outward and the activities allowed in each
questions.question: A biosphere reserve is divided into zones. Going from the centre outward, which order of zones and allowed activities is correct?
options: A) Transition zone (settlements, farming) → buffer zone (research, education) → core zone (no human activity)
B) Buffer zone (no human activity) → core zone (research, education) → transition zone (settlements, farming)
C) Core zone (settlements, farming) → buffer zone (research, education) → transition zone (no human activity)
D) Core zone (strictly protected, no human interference) → buffer zone (limited activities such as research and education) → transition zone (human settlements, farming and other uses)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Core zone (strictly protected) → buffer zone (limited research and education) → transition zone (settlements and farming).
Concept: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat, through biodiversity hotspots, biosphere reserves, national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and sacred groves. A biosphere reserve combines strict protection with human use in zones.
Why: The core zone at the centre is kept free of human disturbance. Around it, the buffer zone allows limited activities that do not harm the core. The outermost transition zone allows people to live and use resources in ways that support conservation.
Why not the others: (A) This gives the correct zones but in the order from outside to inside. (B) The buffer zone is not the strictly protected centre; the core is. (C) Settlements are allowed in the outer transition zone, not in the core.
Key point: Biosphere reserve: core (protected) → buffer (limited use) → transition (human use).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Estimating the length of TMV RNA from its coat-protein subunits and comparing it with a viroid
questions.question: A tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) particle is a rod in which 2130 identical coat-protein subunits surround a single RNA strand, each subunit binding 3 nucleotides of the RNA. A typical viroid has about 359 nucleotides. About how many nucleotides does the TMV RNA have, about how many times longer is it than the viroid RNA, and how does the viroid differ in structure?
options: A) 2130 nucleotides; about 6 times; the viroid has a lipid envelope
B) About 6400 nucleotides; about 18 times; the viroid is a free RNA with no protein coat
C) About 6400 nucleotides; about 18 times; the viroid has a protein coat but no RNA
D) 710 nucleotides; about 2 times; the viroid is double-stranded DNA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) About 6400 nucleotides; about 18 times; the viroid is a free RNA with no protein coat.
Concept: Viruses have nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) inside a protein coat (capsid); TMV, a plant virus, has single-stranded RNA. Viroids, discovered by T.O. Diener as the cause of potato spindle tuber disease, are small free RNA molecules without a protein coat, and much smaller than viral genomes.
Given: 2130 subunits; 3 nucleotides per subunit; viroid = 359 nucleotides.
Formula/Principle: RNA length = number of subunits × nucleotides per subunit.
Step 1: 2130 × 3 = 6390 ≈ 6400 nucleotides.
Step 2: 6390 ÷ 359 ≈ 17.8 ≈ 18 times.
Why: The protein subunits are arranged in a helix along the RNA, so the number of subunits sets the RNA length. A viroid is only infectious RNA.
Why not the others: (A) Takes the number of subunits as the number of nucleotides; also, viroids have no envelope. (C) A viroid is RNA with no protein, the opposite of this statement. (D) Divides by 3 instead of multiplying; viroids are RNA, not DNA.
Key point: TMV RNA ≈ 2130 × 3 ≈ 6400 nucleotides; a viroid is naked RNA of a few hundred nucleotides.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Placing a marine worm-like animal with proboscis, collar and stomochord in its phylum
questions.question: A marine worm-like animal has a body in three regions (proboscis, collar and trunk). It has pharyngeal gill slits, an open circulatory system, excretion by a proboscis gland, and a short rod-like structure in the proboscis called a stomochord. To which group does it belong?
options: A) Hemichordata, a non-chordate group, because the stomochord is not a true notochord
B) Annelida, because it is worm-like with a body in regions
C) Chordata, because the stomochord is a notochord
D) Echinodermata, because it is marine and has an open circulatory system
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Hemichordata, a non-chordate group, because the stomochord is not a true notochord.
Concept: Hemichordates (for example Balanoglossus, Saccoglossus) are worm-like marine animals with a body of proboscis, collar and trunk. They have gill slits and an open circulatory system, and excrete by a proboscis gland. Their stomochord resembles a notochord but is now placed with the non-chordates.
Why: The three-part body, proboscis gland and stomochord are the defining features of Hemichordata.
Why not the others: (B) Annelids are metamerically segmented, excrete by nephridia and have a closed circulatory system. (C) A true notochord is a rod along the back of the body; the stomochord is a small outgrowth of the gut in the proboscis. (D) Echinoderms have a water-vascular system and tube feet, with radial symmetry in adults.
Key point: Proboscis–collar–trunk, stomochord, proboscis gland → Hemichordata (non-chordate).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Why stomata are mostly on the lower surface of a dorsiventral leaf but on both surfaces of an isobilateral leaf
questions.question: In a sunflower (dicot) leaf most stomata lie on the lower surface, while in a maize (monocot) leaf they are about equally distributed on both surfaces. What explains this difference?
options: A) The lower surface of a dicot leaf has palisade mesophyll, which needs more CO₂
B) Monocot leaves have no mesophyll, so stomata can be placed anywhere
C) Stomata on the lower surface absorb CO₂ given off by the soil

D) The dicot leaf is dorsiventral and held roughly horizontal, so its upper surface receives direct sunlight and is hotter; fewer stomata there reduce water loss. The monocot leaf is isobilateral and held more upright, so both surfaces are similarly exposed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) The dicot leaf is dorsiventral and held horizontally, so fewer stomata on its sunlit upper surface reduce water loss; the isobilateral monocot leaf is held upright, with both surfaces similarly exposed.
Concept: A dorsiventral (dicot) leaf has palisade mesophyll under the upper epidermis and spongy mesophyll above the lower epidermis, and usually more stomata on the lower (abaxial) surface. An isobilateral (monocot) leaf has similar upper and lower sides, undifferentiated mesophyll and stomata on both surfaces.
Why: Transpiration is greater from a surface that is heated by direct sunlight. Placing most stomata on the shaded lower surface lets gas exchange continue while limiting water loss. An upright leaf gets light on both sides, so both surfaces have stomata.
Why not the others: (A) The palisade layer lies under the upper epidermis, not the lower; and CO₂ diffuses through the air spaces to all mesophyll cells. (B) Monocot leaves do have mesophyll; it is simply not divided into palisade and spongy layers. (C) Leaves take CO₂ from the surrounding air; stomata are not placed to collect gas from the soil.
Key point: Dorsiventral leaf → stomata mostly on the lower surface; isobilateral leaf → stomata on both surfaces.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Fate of a chromosome fragment without a centromere at the next cell division
questions.question: X-rays break a chromosome in a dividing cell, producing a fragment that has no centromere. What is the most likely fate of this fragment at the next division?
options: A) It moves to the poles normally, because spindle fibres attach to the telomeres at its ends
B) It forms a new centromere and becomes an extra complete chromosome
C) It has no kinetochore, so spindle fibres cannot attach to it; it fails to move to a pole at anaphase and is usually lost from the daughter nuclei
D) It becomes the satellite of another chromosome at the nucleolar organiser
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) It has no kinetochore, so spindle fibres cannot attach; it fails to move to a pole and is usually lost.
Concept: The centromere is the primary constriction of a chromosome. Disc-shaped kinetochores form on its sides, and spindle fibres attach to them to pull the chromatids to the poles at anaphase.
Why: Without a centromere, the fragment has no kinetochore, so it is not pulled to either pole. It lags behind, is left outside the reforming nuclei, and is lost. The daughter cells therefore carry a deletion of that segment.
Why not the others: (A) Spindle fibres attach at kinetochores on the centromere, not at the telomeres. (B) A broken fragment cannot make a new centromere; its replicated copy still has none. (D) A satellite is a small normal segment beyond the secondary constriction of certain chromosomes; it is not formed from broken fragments.
Key point: No centromere → no kinetochore → no spindle attachment → fragment lost at division.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Formula, coordination number and number of ions in solution from the IUPAC name of an oxalato complex
questions.question: What is the formula of potassium trioxalatochromate(III), what is the coordination number of chromium in it, and how many moles of ions in total are present when 0.010 mol of the compound is dissolved in water (assume complete dissociation into the complex ion and the counter-ions)?
options: A) K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]; coordination number 3; 0.040 mol
B) K[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]; coordination number 6; 0.020 mol
C) K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]; coordination number 6; 0.040 mol
D) K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]; coordination number 6; 0.070 mol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃]; coordination number 6; 0.040 mol.
Concept: In an IUPAC name the cation is named first. "Trioxalato" means three oxalate ligands (C₂O₄²⁻), each bidentate (bonding through two O atoms). The ending "-ate" shows that the complex is an anion; (III) is the oxidation state of the metal.
Given: three C₂O₄²⁻ ligands; Cr in the +3 state; 0.010 mol of compound.
Formula/Principle: charge of complex = oxidation state of metal + sum of ligand charges; coordination number = number of donor atoms bonded to the metal.
Step 1: Charge = +3 + 3(−2) = −3, so three K⁺ ions are needed: K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃].
Step 2: Coordination number = 3 ligands × 2 donor atoms = 6.
Step 3: K₃[Cr(C₂O₄)₃] → 3K⁺ + [Cr(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻, giving 4 ions per formula unit; 0.010 × 4 = 0.040 mol of ions.
Why: The ligands stay bonded to chromium in solution; only the K⁺ ions separate from the complex anion.
Why not the others: (A) Counts ligands, not donor atoms; oxalate is bidentate. (B) With three oxalates the complex has charge −3, so it needs three K⁺, not one. (D) Treats the oxalates and Cr³⁺ as separate free ions; the complex ion does not break up.
Key point: Charge balance fixes the formula; bidentate ligands count twice in the coordination number; the complex ion stays as one ion.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ease of dehydrohalogenation of primary, secondary and tertiary bromides and the major alkene from 2-bromo-2-methylbutane
questions.question: Haloalkanes are heated with alcoholic KOH. What is the order of ease of dehydrohalogenation of 1-bromopropane (1°), 2-bromopropane (2°) and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3°), and what is the major alkene formed from 2-bromo-2-methylbutane?
options: A) 3° > 2° > 1°; 2-methylbut-2-ene
B) 1° > 2° > 3°; 2-methylbut-1-ene
C) 3° > 2° > 1°; 2-methylbut-1-ene
D) 1° > 2° > 3°; 2-methylbut-2-ene
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3° > 2° > 1°; 2-methylbut-2-ene.
Concept: With alcoholic KOH (a strong base in a less polar solvent) elimination is favoured; with aqueous KOH, substitution is favoured. Elimination removes H from a β-carbon and X from the α-carbon. Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule: the more substituted alkene (with more alkyl groups on the double-bond carbons) is the major product.
Why: A tertiary halide has more β-hydrogens and gives a more substituted, more stable alkene, and its crowded carbon resists substitution, so it eliminates most easily. In 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, (CH₃)₂CBr–CH₂–CH₃, removing H from the CH₂ gives (CH₃)₂C=CH–CH₃ (trisubstituted), the major product; removing H from a CH₃ gives CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ (disubstituted), the minor product.
Why not the others: (B) Reverses the order of ease and gives the less substituted (minor) alkene. (C) The order is right, but 2-methylbut-1-ene is the minor product. (D) The product is right, but primary halides eliminate least readily.
Key point: Ease of elimination 3° > 2° > 1°; Saytzeff: the more substituted alkene is the major product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Products of acid-catalysed hydration and hydroboration–oxidation of 3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene
questions.question: 3,3-Dimethylbut-1-ene, (CH₃)₃C–CH=CH₂, is converted to alcohols by two methods: (i) hydration with dilute H₂SO₄, and (ii) hydroboration–oxidation (B₂H₆, then H₂O₂/OH⁻). What is the major product of each?
options: A) (i) 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol; (ii) 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol
B) (i) 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, formed after a methyl shift; (ii) 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol
C) (i) 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol; (ii) 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol
D) (i) 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol; (ii) 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (i) 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol, formed after a methyl shift; (ii) 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
Concept: Acid-catalysed hydration goes through a carbocation (Markovnikov addition), and a carbocation can rearrange to a more stable one by a 1,2-shift. Hydroboration–oxidation adds H and OH without a carbocation, placing OH on the less substituted carbon (anti-Markovnikov overall) with no rearrangement.
Why: (i) H⁺ adds to CH₂, giving the secondary cation (CH₃)₃C–C⁺H–CH₃. A methyl group shifts from the next carbon, giving the more stable tertiary cation (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. Water attacks it, giving (CH₃)₂C(OH)–CH(CH₃)₂, 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol. (ii) Boron adds to the terminal CH₂; oxidation replaces B by OH, giving (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–CH₂OH, 3,3-dimethylbutan-1-ol.
Why not the others: (A) The secondary cation rearranges before water attacks, so the unrearranged secondary alcohol is not the major product of (i). (C) Hydroboration–oxidation puts OH on the terminal carbon, not on C-2. (D) The two products are swapped.
Key point: Acid hydration → carbocation → possible rearrangement; hydroboration–oxidation → anti-Markovnikov, no rearrangement.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Which named reactions give benzaldehyde and which give other products
questions.question:
Consider these reactions.
(i) Toluene + chromyl chloride (CrO₂Cl₂) in CS₂, then H₃O⁺
(ii) Benzene + CO + HCl with anhydrous AlCl₃/CuCl
(iii) Benzonitrile + SnCl₂/HCl, then H₃O⁺
(iv) Benzoyl chloride + H₂ over Pd on BaSO₄
(v) Toluene + alkaline KMnO₄, then acidification
(vi) Benzoyl chloride + LiAlH₄, then H₂O
How many of them give benzaldehyde as the main product?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4.
Concept: Aldehydes are easily oxidised to acids and easily reduced to alcohols, so a method for preparing an aldehyde must stop at the aldehyde stage. Named methods do this: Etard reaction, Gattermann–Koch reaction, Stephen reaction and Rosenmund reduction.
Why: (i) Etard: chromyl chloride forms a chromium complex that is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde. (ii) Gattermann–Koch: formylation of benzene gives benzaldehyde. (iii) Stephen: the nitrile is reduced to an imine, which is hydrolysed to benzaldehyde. (iv) Rosenmund: the poisoned catalyst reduces the acid chloride only to the aldehyde. (v) Strong oxidation of toluene goes all the way to benzoic acid. (vi) LiAlH₄ reduces the acid chloride all the way to benzyl alcohol. So (i)–(iv) give benzaldehyde.
Why not the others: (A) Includes (v) and (vi), which overshoot to the acid and to the alcohol. (B) Misses one of the four named aldehyde preparations. (C) Includes one of the over-oxidation or over-reduction reactions.
Key point: Etard, Gattermann–Koch, Stephen and Rosenmund stop at the aldehyde; KMnO₄ overshoots to the acid and LiAlH₄ to the alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Diazotisation, Sandmeyer cyanation and hydrolysis: aniline to benzoic acid, and why diazotisation is done cold
questions.question: Aniline is converted in three steps: aniline → X (NaNO₂ + HCl at 273–278 K) → Y (CuCN/KCN) → Z (H₃O⁺, heat). What are X, Y and Z, and why is the first step carried out at 273–278 K?
options: A) X = benzenediazonium chloride, Y = phenyl isocyanide, Z = aniline; the low temperature prevents the formation of nitrobenzene
B) X = benzenediazonium chloride, Y = benzonitrile, Z = benzoic acid; the low temperature is needed because the diazonium salt decomposes on warming (to phenol and N₂)
C) X = nitrobenzene, Y = benzonitrile, Z = benzamide; the low temperature prevents the escape of HCl
D) X = benzenediazonium chloride, Y = benzonitrile, Z = benzylamine; the low temperature increases the rate of diazotisation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) X = benzenediazonium chloride, Y = benzonitrile, Z = benzoic acid; the cold prevents the diazonium salt from decomposing.
Concept: Primary aromatic amines react with nitrous acid (from NaNO₂ + HCl) in the cold to give arenediazonium salts. These are useful intermediates: in the Sandmeyer reaction, CuCN/KCN replaces –N₂⁺ by –CN. Nitriles are hydrolysed by acid to carboxylic acids.
Why: C₆H₅NH₂ → C₆H₅N₂⁺Cl⁻ (X) → C₆H₅CN (Y) + N₂ → C₆H₅COOH (Z) on hydrolysis. Benzenediazonium chloride is stable only in the cold; when warmed in water it gives phenol and nitrogen gas, so it is made and used at 273–278 K.
Why not the others: (A) CuCN gives a nitrile (–C≡N) bonded through carbon, not an isocyanide; and hydrolysis of the cyanide group does not regenerate aniline. (C) Nitrous acid diazotises the amine; it does not form nitrobenzene; full acid hydrolysis goes past the amide to the acid. (D) Hydrolysis of a nitrile gives an acid; benzylamine would need reduction of the nitrile. The low temperature is for stability, not speed.
Key point: ArNH₂ → ArN₂⁺ (cold) → ArCN (Sandmeyer) → ArCOOH (hydrolysis).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why RNA is hydrolysed by dilute alkali but DNA is not
questions.question: RNA is readily hydrolysed when kept in dilute aqueous alkali, while DNA under the same conditions is hardly affected. Which statement explains this?
options: A) DNA is less stable than RNA because thymine carries an extra methyl group
B) RNA is more stable than DNA because it is single-stranded
C) The 2′-OH group of ribose in RNA can attack the neighbouring phosphodiester bond and break it; deoxyribose in DNA has no 2′-OH group, so DNA is more stable
D) Both are hydrolysed equally, because both have the same sugar–phosphate backbone
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The 2′-OH of ribose in RNA attacks the neighbouring phosphodiester bond; DNA's deoxyribose lacks the 2′-OH, so DNA is more stable.
Concept: Nucleic acids are polymers of nucleotides joined by 3′–5′ phosphodiester bonds. RNA contains β-D-ribose; DNA contains β-D-2-deoxyribose, which has H in place of OH at carbon 2′. DNA uses thymine where RNA uses uracil.
Why: In alkali, the 2′-OH of ribose loses H⁺, and the resulting O⁻ attacks the phosphorus of the adjacent 3′-phosphodiester bond, breaking the chain. DNA cannot do this, which is one reason DNA is the more stable store of genetic information.
Why not the others: (A) The observation is that DNA is the more stable one; the methyl group of thymine does not cause alkaline hydrolysis. (B) The observation shows RNA is the less stable one, and the reason is chemical (the 2′-OH), not the number of strands. (D) The sugars differ (ribose versus deoxyribose), and this difference explains the different behaviour.
Key point: The 2′-OH makes RNA alkali-labile; 2′-deoxyribose makes DNA chemically stable.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking mixtures of aluminium and chlorine by the amount of AlCl₃ formed, using the limiting reagent
questions.question:
Aluminium reacts with chlorine: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃. Four mixtures react completely:
(i) 2.7 g Al + 7.1 g Cl₂
(ii) 5.4 g Al + 7.1 g Cl₂
(iii) 2.7 g Al + 21.3 g Cl₂
(iv) 1.35 g Al + 14.2 g Cl₂
What is the order of the amount of AlCl₃ formed? (Al = 27, Cl = 35.5)
options: A) (ii) > (i) > (iii) > (iv)
B) (iii) > (iv) > (i) = (ii)
C) (iii) > (ii) > (i) > (iv)
D) (iii) > (i) = (ii) > (iv)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (iii) > (i) = (ii) > (iv).
Concept: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is used up first; it fixes the amount of product. Compare the mole ratio of the reactants with the ratio in the equation (Al : Cl₂ = 2 : 3).
Given: Al = 27 g mol⁻¹; Cl₂ = 71 g mol⁻¹; 2 mol Al reacts with 3 mol Cl₂ to give 2 mol AlCl₃.
Formula/Principle: mol AlCl₃ = smaller of (mol Al) and (2/3 × mol Cl₂).
Step 1: (i) Al 0.10, Cl₂ 0.10 → 2/3 × 0.10 = 0.067 mol (Cl₂ limiting). (ii) Al 0.20, Cl₂ 0.10 → 0.067 mol (Cl₂ limiting).
Step 2: (iii) Al 0.10, Cl₂ 0.30 → 0.10 mol (Al limiting). (iv) Al 0.050, Cl₂ 0.20 → 0.050 mol (Al limiting).
Why: Adding more of the reagent that is already in excess (Al in (ii)) does not increase the product.
Why not the others: (A) Assumes more Al always gives more product, ignoring that Cl₂ limits (i) and (ii). (B) Ranks by mass of Cl₂, but in (iv) the small amount of Al limits the product. (C) Treats (ii) as giving more than (i), but extra excess Al gives no extra product.
Key point: Product depends only on the limiting reagent; excess reagent does not add product.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Identifying an orbital from the number of radial nodes in its radial probability graph and one angular node
questions.question: The figure shows the radial probability distribution of one orbital of the hydrogen atom against the distance r from the nucleus. This orbital also has exactly one angular nodal plane. Which orbital is it, and what are its principal and azimuthal quantum numbers?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 4p; n = 4, l = 1.
Concept: An orbital with quantum numbers n and l has n − l − 1 radial nodes (spherical surfaces where the probability is zero) and l angular nodes (nodal planes or cones). A radial probability curve shows radial nodes as points (other than r = 0) where the curve falls to zero.
Why: The graph touches zero twice (apart from the nucleus), so there are 2 radial nodes: n − l − 1 = 2. One angular nodal plane means l = 1 (a p orbital). Then n = 2 + l + 1 = 4, so the orbital is 4p. It can hold at most 2 electrons, and m can be −1, 0 or +1.
Why not the others: (B) 3s has 2 radial nodes, but l = 0 means no angular node. (C) 3p has 3 − 1 − 1 = 1 radial node only. (D) 4d has 4 − 2 − 1 = 1 radial node and 2 angular nodes.
Key point: Radial nodes = n − l − 1; angular nodes = l; total nodes = n − 1.
questions.image_alt: Graph of radial probability against distance r from the nucleus for one orbital of the hydrogen atom. The curve starts at zero at the nucleus, rises to a small first maximum, falls to zero at a first node, rises to a larger second maximum, falls to zero at a second node, and then rises to the largest third maximum farther out before falling gradually towards zero. Apart from r = 0 the curve touches zero exactly twice.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: Why lithium is the strongest reducing agent among alkali metals in water despite its high ionisation enthalpy
questions.question: Lithium has the highest first ionisation enthalpy in group 1, yet its standard electrode potential, E°(Li⁺/Li) = −3.04 V, is the most negative, so lithium is the strongest reducing agent among the alkali metals in aqueous solution. Which statement explains this?
options: A) Lithium has the lowest ionisation enthalpy in the group
B) Lithium has the largest atomic radius in the group
C) The very small Li⁺ ion has the largest (most negative) hydration enthalpy, which more than makes up for its higher ionisation enthalpy
D) The Li⁺ ion has the smallest hydrated radius, so it moves away from the electrode fastest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The very small Li⁺ ion has the most negative hydration enthalpy, which outweighs its higher ionisation enthalpy.
Concept: The reducing power in water depends on the overall change M(s) → M⁺(aq) + e⁻, which includes sublimation enthalpy, ionisation enthalpy and hydration enthalpy. Hydration enthalpy becomes more negative as ion size decreases.
Why: Li⁺ is the smallest alkali-metal ion and has the highest charge density, so it is very strongly hydrated (it releases much energy in water). This large release of energy more than makes up for the extra energy needed to ionise lithium, so the overall process is most favourable for Li.
Why not the others: (A) Ionisation enthalpy decreases down the group; lithium's is the highest. (B) Atomic radius increases down the group; lithium is the smallest. (D) Because Li⁺ is so strongly hydrated, its hydrated ion is the largest and moves most slowly in water.
Key point: In water, the large hydration enthalpy of small Li⁺ makes Li the strongest reducing agent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Paramagnetism and bond-order order of B₂, C₂, N₂, O₂ and F₂ from molecular orbital theory
questions.question: Using molecular orbital theory (with s–p mixing for B₂, C₂ and N₂), which statement about B₂, C₂, N₂, O₂ and F₂ is correct?
options: A) B₂ and O₂ are paramagnetic; the bond orders are N₂ > C₂ = O₂ > B₂ = F₂
B) Only O₂ is paramagnetic; the bond orders are N₂ > O₂ > C₂ > F₂ > B₂
C) B₂, C₂ and O₂ are paramagnetic; the bond orders are N₂ > C₂ = O₂ > B₂ = F₂
D) B₂ and O₂ are paramagnetic; the bond orders are O₂ > N₂ > C₂ > B₂ = F₂
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) B₂ and O₂ are paramagnetic; N₂ > C₂ = O₂ > B₂ = F₂.
Concept: Bond order = ½(bonding electrons − antibonding electrons). For B₂, C₂ and N₂, the π2p orbitals lie below σ2p (s–p mixing); for O₂ and F₂, σ2p lies below π2p. A molecule with unpaired electrons is paramagnetic.
Why: B₂ (6 valence electrons): σ2s² σ*2s² π2p¹ π2p¹, two unpaired electrons, bond order 1. C₂ (8): π2p⁴ all paired, bond order 2, diamagnetic. N₂ (10): bond order 3. O₂ (12): two unpaired electrons in π*2p, bond order 2. F₂ (14): bond order 1, diamagnetic.
Why not the others: (B) B₂ is also paramagnetic, and C₂ and O₂ have equal bond orders (2). (C) With π2p below σ2p, C₂ fills π2p⁴ with all electrons paired, so it is diamagnetic. (D) N₂ has the highest bond order (3), above O₂ (2).
Key point: Paramagnetic: B₂ and O₂; bond orders: B₂ 1, C₂ 2, N₂ 3, O₂ 2, F₂ 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Fraction of air expelled from an open flask on heating, and the pressure after sealing and cooling
questions.question: An open flask containing air at 27 °C and 1.0 atm is heated to 477 °C, keeping the pressure at 1.0 atm (air leaves through the mouth). The flask is then sealed and cooled back to 27 °C. What fraction of the original air was expelled, and what is the final pressure in the sealed flask? (Neglect the expansion of the flask.)
options: A) 40 % expelled; 0.60 atm
B) 60 % expelled; 0.40 atm
C) 94 % expelled; 0.057 atm
D) 60 % expelled; 1.0 atm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 60 % expelled; 0.40 atm.
Concept: At constant pressure and volume, the amount of gas in a vessel is inversely proportional to its absolute temperature (n ∝ 1/T, from PV = nRT). In a sealed rigid vessel, the pressure is proportional to nT.
Given: T₁ = 300 K, T₂ = 750 K, P = 1.0 atm, V constant.
Formula/Principle: n₂/n₁ = T₁/T₂ at constant P and V; in the sealed rigid flask, P ∝ nT.
Step 1: n₂/n₁ = 300/750 = 0.40, so 40 % of the air remains and 60 % is expelled.
Step 2: The sealed flask now holds 0.40 n₁ at 300 K in the same volume, so P = 0.40 × 1.0 atm = 0.40 atm.
Why: Heating at constant pressure drives gas out; on cooling the remaining smaller amount of gas exerts a lower pressure.
Why not the others: (A) Swaps the fraction remaining and the fraction expelled. (C) Uses Celsius temperatures (27/477) instead of kelvin. (D) Ignores the fact that less gas at the same temperature in the same volume gives a lower pressure.
Key point: Always use kelvin; at fixed P and V, n ∝ 1/T; in a sealed rigid flask, P ∝ nT.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Selective precipitation of AgCl before Ag₂CrO₄ and the chloride left when chromate starts to precipitate
questions.question: Silver nitrate solution is added slowly to a solution containing 0.10 M Cl⁻ and 0.010 M CrO₄²⁻ (neglect volume change). Ksp(AgCl) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰; Ksp(Ag₂CrO₄) = 1.1 × 10⁻¹². Which salt precipitates first, and what is the chloride concentration when the second salt starts to precipitate?
options: A) Ag₂CrO₄ precipitates first, because its Ksp is smaller
B) Both start to precipitate together at [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M
C) AgCl precipitates first; when Ag₂CrO₄ begins, [Cl⁻] ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M
D) AgCl precipitates first, at [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M; Ag₂CrO₄ begins at [Ag⁺] ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, when [Cl⁻] has fallen to ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) AgCl first at [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M; Ag₂CrO₄ begins at [Ag⁺] ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ M, when [Cl⁻] ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Concept: A salt precipitates when its ionic product exceeds Ksp. The salt that needs the smaller [Ag⁺] precipitates first. Ksp values cannot be compared directly when the salts have different formula types (AgCl is 1 : 1, Ag₂CrO₄ is 2 : 1).
Given: [Cl⁻] = 0.10 M; [CrO₄²⁻] = 0.010 M; Ksp values as stated.
Formula/Principle: AgCl: [Ag⁺] = Ksp/[Cl⁻]; Ag₂CrO₄: [Ag⁺] = √(Ksp/[CrO₄²⁻]).
Step 1: For AgCl: [Ag⁺] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M.
Step 2: For Ag₂CrO₄: [Ag⁺] = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹²/0.010) = √(1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰) ≈ 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Step 3: When [Ag⁺] reaches 1.05 × 10⁻⁵ M, [Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰/1.05 × 10⁻⁵ ≈ 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ M.
Why: AgCl needs far less Ag⁺, so it precipitates first; by the time chromate starts to precipitate (red Ag₂CrO₄), almost all the chloride (over 99.98 %) has been removed. This is the basis of chloride titration with chromate as indicator.
Why not the others: (A) Comparing Ksp values directly is wrong for salts of different formula types; the [Ag⁺] needed is what matters. (B) The two salts need very different [Ag⁺] values. (C) 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M is the [Ag⁺] at which AgCl starts, not the [Cl⁻] left.
Key point: Compare the [Ag⁺] each salt needs, not the Ksp values, when the formula types differ.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Common-ion effect of NH₄Cl on NH₄OH in the precipitation of group III hydroxides
questions.question: In qualitative analysis, NH₄Cl is added before NH₄OH to precipitate the hydroxides of Fe³⁺, Al³⁺ and Cr³⁺ (group III). Why is NH₄Cl added?
options: A) NH₄⁺ (a common ion) suppresses the ionisation of NH₄OH, lowering [OH⁻] so that only the hydroxides with very low Ksp (Fe, Al, Cr) precipitate, while those of Zn²⁺, Mn²⁺, Mg²⁺ and others stay in solution
B) NH₄Cl raises [OH⁻], so that the group III hydroxides precipitate completely
C) NH₄Cl forms soluble complexes with Fe³⁺ and Al³⁺, which then precipitate as hydroxides
D) NH₄Cl makes the solution strongly acidic, so that only amphoteric hydroxides precipitate
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) NH₄⁺ suppresses the ionisation of NH₄OH, lowering [OH⁻] so that only the very insoluble group III hydroxides precipitate.
Concept: Common-ion effect: adding an ion already produced by a weak electrolyte shifts its ionisation equilibrium back, lowering the concentration of the other ion. NH₄OH ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻.
Why: Extra NH₄⁺ from the strong electrolyte NH₄Cl pushes this equilibrium to the left, so [OH⁻] becomes small. The ionic products of Fe(OH)₃, Al(OH)₃ and Cr(OH)₃ still exceed their very small Ksp values, but those of Zn(OH)₂, Mn(OH)₂, Mg(OH)₂, Ni(OH)₂ and Co(OH)₂ do not, so these ions remain for later groups.
Why not the others: (B) The common ion lowers [OH⁻]; it does not raise it. (C) NH₄Cl does not complex these ions; they precipitate as hydroxides because their Ksp is exceeded. (D) An NH₄Cl–NH₄OH mixture is a basic buffer, not strongly acidic; strong acid would prevent hydroxide precipitation.
Key point: Common ion NH₄⁺ → lower [OH⁻] → only the least soluble hydroxides precipitate.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Average and actual oxidation numbers of sulphur in the tetrathionate ion and in peroxomonosulphuric acid
questions.question: Which statement about oxidation numbers of sulphur is correct?
options: A) In S₄O₆²⁻ the average oxidation number of S is +2.5, and every S atom is in the +2.5 state
B) In H₂SO₅ the oxidation number of S is +8
C) In S₄O₆²⁻ the average oxidation number of S is +2.5, made up of two S atoms at +5 and two at 0; in H₂SO₅ S is +6, because two of its O atoms form a peroxide link (−1 each)
D) In S₄O₆²⁻ all four S atoms are in the +5 state
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) S₄O₆²⁻: average +2.5 (two S at +5, two at 0); H₂SO₅: S is +6 because of a peroxide link.
Concept: An oxidation number found from the formula alone is an average. When atoms of the same element are in different bonding situations, or when a peroxide (O–O) group is present, the structure must be used.
Why: S₄O₆²⁻: 4x + 6(−2) = −2 gives x = +2.5. In its structure ⁻O₃S–S–S–SO₃⁻, the two central S atoms are bonded only to S (0), and the two end S atoms are bonded to three O each (+5): (2 × 5 + 2 × 0)/4 = 2.5. H₂SO₅ is HO–O–SO₂–OH: taking all O as −2 gives +8, which is impossible for S (only 6 valence electrons); with two O at −1 (peroxide), 2(+1) + x + 3(−2) + 2(−1) = 0 gives x = +6.
Why not the others: (A) Atoms cannot really be in a fractional state; +2.5 is only an average of +5 and 0. (B) S cannot exceed +6, its number of valence electrons; the peroxide O atoms are −1. (D) If all were +5, the ion's charge would be +8, not −2.
Key point: Fractional oxidation numbers are averages; peroxide oxygen is −1, so S in H₂SO₅ is +6.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: Classifying listed species as electrophiles or nucleophiles
questions.question:
The species are listed with labels:

Label | P | Q | R | S | T | U | V
Species | BF₃ | NO₂⁺ | H₂O | CN⁻ | AlCl₃ | (CH₃)₃C⁺ | NH₃

Which classification is correct?
options: A) Electrophiles: P, Q, U; nucleophiles: R, S, T, V
B) Electrophiles: P, Q, T, U; nucleophiles: R, S, V
C) Electrophiles: Q, U only; nucleophiles: P, R, S, T, V
D) Electrophiles: P, T; nucleophiles: Q, R, S, U, V
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Electrophiles: P, Q, T, U; nucleophiles: R, S, V.
Concept: An electrophile ("electron-loving") is an electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair: cations such as NO₂⁺ and carbocations, and neutral molecules with an incomplete octet such as BF₃ and AlCl₃. A nucleophile ("nucleus-loving") has an electron pair to donate: anions such as CN⁻, or neutral molecules with lone pairs such as H₂O and NH₃.
Why: BF₃ and AlCl₃ have only six electrons around B and Al; NO₂⁺ and (CH₃)₃C⁺ are positively charged and electron-deficient. H₂O and NH₃ have lone pairs; CN⁻ is an anion with lone pairs.
Why not the others: (A) AlCl₃ has a vacant orbital on Al and is an electrophile (it is a Lewis acid catalyst). (C) Neutral molecules with an incomplete octet (BF₃, AlCl₃) are electrophiles even though they carry no charge. (D) NO₂⁺ and carbocations have no electron pair to give; they are electrophiles.
Key point: Electron-deficient (cations, incomplete octet) → electrophile; lone pair or negative charge → nucleophile.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Which monosubstituted benzene gives mainly the meta product on nitration, and why
questions.question: Each compound is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. Which one gives mainly the meta-nitro product, and for what reason?
options: A) Anisole, because the –OCH₃ group withdraws electrons by its –I effect
B) Chlorobenzene, because –Cl deactivates the ring
C) Benzaldehyde, because the –CHO group withdraws electrons by its –R effect, making the ortho and para positions more electron-poor than the meta position
D) Toluene, because –CH₃ directs meta by hyperconjugation
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Benzaldehyde, because –CHO withdraws electrons by its –R effect, making the ortho and para positions more electron-poor than meta.
Concept: Substituents on benzene control both the rate and the position of further electrophilic substitution. Electron-donating groups (–OCH₃, –CH₃) activate the ring and direct ortho/para. Groups such as –CHO, –COOH, –NO₂ and –CN withdraw electrons by resonance, deactivate the ring and direct meta. Halogens deactivate (–I) but direct ortho/para (+R).
Why: The resonance structures of benzaldehyde place positive charge at the ortho and para positions. The electrophile NO₂⁺ therefore attacks the meta position, which is the least electron-poor.
Why not the others: (A) –OCH₃ donates electrons by its +R effect, which outweighs its –I effect, so it is ortho/para-directing and activating. (B) –Cl deactivates the ring but its lone pairs direct substitution ortho/para. (D) –CH₃ donates electrons by hyperconjugation and the +I effect, so it directs ortho/para.
Key point: –R groups (–CHO, –COOH, –NO₂, –CN) → meta; activating groups and halogens → ortho/para.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Boiling point and mass of dissolved NaCl from the freezing point of the same solution
questions.question: An aqueous solution of NaCl freezes at −0.93 °C. Assuming complete dissociation of NaCl, at what temperature does the same solution boil at 1 atm, and what mass of NaCl is dissolved per kilogram of water? (Kf = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹, Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹, NaCl = 58.5 g mol⁻¹)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 100.26 °C; 14.6 g.
Concept: Depression of freezing point and elevation of boiling point are colligative properties: they depend on the total molality of solute particles. For an electrolyte, ΔT = i K m, where i is the van 't Hoff factor (i = 2 for fully dissociated NaCl).
Given: ΔTf = 0.93 K; Kf = 1.86; Kb = 0.52 K kg mol⁻¹; i = 2.
Formula/Principle: ΔTf = Kf × (i m); ΔTb = Kb × (i m).
Step 1: i m = 0.93/1.86 = 0.50 mol kg⁻¹ of particles; ΔTb = 0.52 × 0.50 = 0.26 K, so the boiling point is 100.26 °C.
Step 2: m(NaCl) = 0.50/2 = 0.25 mol kg⁻¹; mass = 0.25 × 58.5 = 14.6 g per kg of water.
Why: The same particle molality controls both effects, so ΔTb/ΔTf = Kb/Kf, and the boiling point follows without needing to know i.
Why not the others: (A) The boiling point is right, but taking i = 1 doubles the mass of NaCl. (B) Uses a particle molality of 1.0 for the boiling point, twice the true value. (C) Takes ΔTb equal to ΔTf, ignoring the different constants.
Key point: ΔTb/ΔTf = Kb/Kf for the same solution; divide the particle molality by i to get the salt molality.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Volumes of hydrogen and oxygen at STP from the electrolysis of acidified water
questions.question: Acidified water is electrolysed with inert electrodes using a steady current of 2.00 A for 965 s. What total volume of gas is produced, measured dry at STP, and how is it shared between the electrodes? (F = 96500 C mol⁻¹; molar volume at STP = 22.4 L)
options: A) 224 mL in all: 112 mL H₂ and 112 mL O₂
B) 336 mL in all: 224 mL H₂ at the cathode and 112 mL O₂ at the anode
C) 672 mL in all: 448 mL H₂ at the cathode and 224 mL O₂ at the anode
D) 336 mL in all: 224 mL O₂ at the anode and 112 mL H₂ at the cathode
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 336 mL in all: 224 mL H₂ at the cathode and 112 mL O₂ at the anode.
Concept: Faraday's first law: the amount of substance liberated is proportional to the charge passed. At the cathode 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; at the anode 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
Given: I = 2.00 A; t = 965 s; F = 96500 C mol⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Q = It; mol e⁻ = Q/F; mol H₂ = mol e⁻/2; mol O₂ = mol e⁻/4.
Step 1: Q = 2.00 × 965 = 1930 C; mol e⁻ = 1930/96500 = 0.0200 mol.
Step 2: H₂ = 0.0100 mol = 224 mL; O₂ = 0.00500 mol = 112 mL; total = 336 mL.
Why: Each H₂ needs 2 electrons and each O₂ needs 4, so the volume of hydrogen is twice that of oxygen.
Why not the others: (A) Gives equal volumes, which ignores the different numbers of electrons per molecule. (C) Takes 1 electron per H₂ molecule and 2 per O₂, doubling both. (D) Swaps the gases: hydrogen (reduction) forms at the cathode, oxygen (oxidation) at the anode.
Key point: 2 e⁻ per H₂, 4 e⁻ per O₂; V(H₂) : V(O₂) = 2 : 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Ranking reactions by temperature sensitivity of the rate constant from their activation energies
questions.question: Three reactions have the same pre-exponential factor and activation energies of 50, 100 and 150 kJ mol⁻¹. The temperature is raised from 300 K to 310 K. Which statement about the increase in their rate constants is correct? (R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
options: A) The reaction with Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹ shows the largest relative increase, because its barrier is lowest
B) All three rate constants increase by the same factor, because the temperature rise is the same
C) The order is 150 > 100 > 50 kJ mol⁻¹, and the rate constants increase by factors of about 3, 6 and 9 respectively
D) The order is 150 > 100 > 50 kJ mol⁻¹, and the rate constants increase by factors of about 7.0, 3.6 and 1.9 respectively
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 150 > 100 > 50 kJ mol⁻¹; factors of about 7.0, 3.6 and 1.9.
Concept: Collision theory: only collisions with energy at least Ea (and proper orientation) are effective. The fraction of such collisions is about e^(−Ea/RT), so k = A e^(−Ea/RT). A higher Ea makes this fraction more sensitive to temperature.
Why: k₃₁₀/k₃₀₀ = exp[(Ea/R)(1/300 − 1/310)] = exp(Ea × 1.293 × 10⁻⁵ mol J⁻¹). For 50 kJ: e^0.647 ≈ 1.9; for 100 kJ: e^1.293 ≈ 3.6; for 150 kJ: e^1.94 ≈ 7.0. The factors grow exponentially with Ea (each is the square or cube of the first). The familiar rule that a 10 K rise doubles the rate fits Ea of about 54 kJ mol⁻¹.
Why not the others: (A) A lower barrier means a larger fraction already reacts, so the relative increase is smallest. (B) The factor depends on Ea through the exponent. (C) The order is right, but the factors are not proportional to Ea; they rise exponentially (1.9, 1.9², 1.9³).
Key point: Higher Ea → stronger temperature dependence; ln(k₂/k₁) = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why uranium compounds show many oxidation states while lanthanide compounds are mostly +3
questions.question: In the laboratory, uranium compounds can be prepared with uranium in the +3, +4, +5 and +6 states (for example, yellow UO₂²⁺ salts), whereas compounds of most lanthanides, such as neodymium, are almost always in the +3 state. Which explanation is correct?
options: A) In actinides the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy, so a variable number of electrons can be used in bonding; the 4f electrons of lanthanides are more deeply buried and less available, so +3 is usual
B) Actinides are not radioactive, so they form more stable compounds in high oxidation states
C) Lanthanide atoms are larger than actinide atoms, so they can lose more electrons
D) The 5f electrons of actinides are held more firmly than the 4f electrons of lanthanides, so actinides show fewer oxidation states
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) In actinides the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy, so many oxidation states occur; the deeply buried 4f electrons of lanthanides make +3 usual.
Concept: Lanthanides (4f series) and actinides (5f series) both show +3 as a common state. Actinides show a wider range of oxidation states. They are all radioactive, and the actinide contraction is greater from element to element than the lanthanide contraction because 5f electrons shield poorly.
Why: The 5f orbitals extend farther from the nucleus than 4f orbitals and are close in energy to 6d and 7s, so electrons from all three can take part in bonding. In lanthanides, 4f electrons are well shielded inside the 5s and 5p shells and are hard to remove beyond the third electron.
Why not the others: (B) All actinides are radioactive. (C) Size alone does not explain the range of oxidation states, and the actinide behaviour arises from orbital energies. (D) 5f electrons are held less firmly than 4f electrons, which is why actinides show more oxidation states, not fewer.
Key point: Close 5f–6d–7s energies → many actinide oxidation states; buried 4f → lanthanides mostly +3.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting the relations from A to B that are functions and those that contain a given pair
questions.question: Let A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {p, q}. Of all the relations from A to B, how many are functions from A to B, and how many contain the ordered pair (1, p)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 8; 32.
Given: \(n(A)=3,\ n(B)=2,\ n(A\times B)=6\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a relation is any subset of }A\times B;\ \text{a function assigns exactly one image to each element of }A\)
Step 1: \(\text{functions: each of the 3 elements has 2 choices}\Rightarrow 2^3=8\)
Step 2: \(\text{relations containing }(1,p):\ \text{include it, and choose freely among the other 5 pairs}\Rightarrow 2^5=32\)
Worked derivation: \[\#\text{relations}=2^{6}=64,\quad \#\text{functions}=2^{3}=8,\quad \#\{R\ni(1,p)\}=\tfrac12\cdot64=32\]
Check: \[\text{exactly half of all subsets contain a given element: }64/2=32\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{a function needs one pair for each element of }A\text{, so it is a selection of images, not an arbitrary subset}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{uses }3^2\text{, which counts functions from }B\text{ to }A\); (C) \(\text{64 is the number of all relations, not those containing }(1,p)\); (D) \(\text{6 is the number of ordered pairs in }A\times B\).
Key point: \(\#\text{relations}=2^{mn};\ \#\text{functions }A\to B=n^{m}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain and range of the sum of two square roots using a quarter circle
questions.question: What are the domain and the range of the real function \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{5-x}\)?
options: A) Domain \([1,5]\); range \([0,2\sqrt2]\)
C) Domain \((1,5)\); range \([2,2\sqrt2]\)
D) Domain \([1,5]\); range \([2,2\sqrt2]\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Domain \([1,5]\); range \([2,2\sqrt2]\).
Given: \(f(x)=\sqrt{x-1}+\sqrt{5-x}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{put }u=\sqrt{x-1},\ v=\sqrt{5-x}\ (u,v\ge0);\ \text{then }u^2+v^2=4\text{, a quarter circle of radius 2}\)
Step 1: \(\text{domain: }x-1\ge0\text{ and }5-x\ge0\Rightarrow 1\le x\le5\)
Step 2: \(f=u+v;\ (u+v)^2=u^2+v^2+2uv=4+2uv,\ \text{with }0\le uv\le\tfrac{u^2+v^2}{2}=2\)
Worked derivation: \[4\le (u+v)^2\le 8\ \Rightarrow\ 2\le f(x)\le2\sqrt2\]
Check: \[f(1)=0+2=2,\quad f(5)=2+0=2,\quad f(3)=\sqrt2+\sqrt2=2\sqrt2\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the line }u+v=c\text{ meets the quarter circle for }2\le c\le2\sqrt2\text{: lowest at the end points of the arc, highest where it touches at }u=v\)
Why not the others: (A) \(f\text{ is a sum of two non-negative roots that cannot both vanish, so it never reaches 0}\); (B) \(u+v=4\text{ would need }uv=6>2\text{, impossible}\); (C) \(x=1\text{ and }x=5\text{ are allowed, since }\sqrt0=0\).
Key point: \(\text{substitute to see a circle: }u^2+v^2=\text{const}\Rightarrow u+v\text{ ranges between the radius and }\sqrt2\times\text{radius}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Angular speed in radians, arc distance of a rim point and its position after a given time
questions.question: A wheel of radius 35 cm turns at 300 revolutions per minute. What is its angular speed in radians per second, what distance does a point on the rim travel each second, and where is a rim point that starts at the rightmost position (angle 0, turning anticlockwise) after 0.35 s?
options: A) \(10\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\); \(350\pi\ \text{cm}\approx 11.0\ \text{m}\); at the lowest point of the wheel
B) \(300\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\); \(105\ \text{m}\); at the highest point
C) \(5\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\); \(175\pi\ \text{cm}\); at the leftmost point
D) \(10\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\); \(350\ \text{cm}\); at the highest point
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(10\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\); \(350\pi\ \text{cm}\approx11.0\ \text{m}\); at the lowest point.
Given: \(r=35\ \text{cm},\ 300\ \text{rev min}^{-1},\ t=0.35\ \text{s}\)
Formula/Principle: \(1\ \text{rev}=2\pi\ \text{rad};\ \text{arc length }s=r\theta\)
Step 1: \(\omega=\dfrac{300\times2\pi}{60}=10\pi\ \text{rad s}^{-1}\)
Step 2: \(s=r\omega t=35\times10\pi\times1=350\pi\ \text{cm}\approx1100\ \text{cm}\)
Worked derivation: \[\theta(0.35)=10\pi\times0.35=3.5\pi=2\pi+\tfrac{3\pi}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ (\cos\theta,\sin\theta)=(0,-1)\]
Check: \[350\pi\approx350\times3.1416=1099.6\ \text{cm}\approx11.0\ \text{m}\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{an angle of }3\pi/2\text{ measured anticlockwise from the positive }x\text{-axis points straight down}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\text{300 is revolutions per minute, not radians per second}\); (C) \(\text{uses }\pi\text{ rad per revolution instead of }2\pi\); (D) \(\text{forgets the factor }\pi\text{ in }s=r\theta\text{, and }3\pi/2\text{ is the bottom, not the top}\).
Key point: \(\omega(\text{rad s}^{-1})=2\pi\times\text{rpm}/60;\ s=r\theta\text{ with }\theta\text{ in radians}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Finding a complex number from an equation in z and its conjugate
questions.question: A complex number z satisfies \(z+2\bar z=3-i\). What is z, and what is its modulus?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) \(1+i\); \(\sqrt2\).
Given: \(z+2\bar z=3-i\)
Formula/Principle: \(z=x+iy,\ \bar z=x-iy;\ \text{equate real and imaginary parts}\)
Step 1: \(x+iy+2x-2iy=3x-iy\)
Step 2: \(3x-iy=3-i\Rightarrow x=1,\ y=1\)
Worked derivation: \[z=1+i,\qquad |z|=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2\]
Check: \[(1+i)+2(1-i)=3-i\ \checkmark\]
Why: \(\text{the conjugate changes the sign of }y\text{, so the two parts give separate equations}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{gets the sign of }y\text{ wrong: }(1-i)+2(1+i)=3+i\); (B) \(\text{treats }\bar z\text{ as }z\text{ and divides by 3}\); (D) \(\text{gives }(-1+i)+2(-1-i)=-3-i\).
Key point: \(\text{write }z=x+iy\text{ and compare real and imaginary parts}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Number of sides of a polygon from its diagonals, and triangles from its vertices (nCr versus nPr)
questions.question: A convex polygon has 54 diagonals. How many sides does it have, and how many triangles can be formed using its vertices?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 12; 220.
Given: \(\text{diagonals}=54\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{diagonals}=\binom n2-n=\dfrac{n(n-3)}{2};\ \ ^nP_r=r!\,\binom nr\)
